So the generator still exits 0 with holes in the output. Only `test_recompiler.cpp:58` reads the result.
- **Missing cases:** `PPC_INST_VRLW`, `VPKUHUM`, `VRFIP`, `VMAXSB`, `VCMPGTSW`, `VCMPEQUH`, `LFDU`, `STFSU`, `FCTIW`, `FCMPO`, `FNMADD`, `MTFSB0` and `MTVSCR` each have 0 case labels in recompiler.cpp.

verify.corrected_gain: No fps gain, which matches the finding. It is a correctness and safety improvement for non-FM2 titles. FM2 output would not change. Making the generator return a non-zero exit code on unrecognized instructions is nearly free (check the `Recompile(fn)` result at line 2791). That is the highest-value, lowest-effort part.
verify.blockers: None. The effort-M estimate is plausible if the full VMX set is implemented. Doing only the loud-failure change plus the CR6 fix for VCMPGTUB/VCMPGTUH is closer to S. Per-opcode unit tests against Xenia's emitter would be needed to catch element-order errors.

title: Optional policy: a single MXCSR mode (always FTZ+DAZ) removes every switch, with a cheap probe to prove it is safe for a given game
evidence: Today 1,909 real ldmxcsr sites and 19,441 conditional checks are emitted (sim.pl), about 21.3k sites at roughly 8.7 host instructions each (f1.asm, 19 sites). Scalar-FPU denormals are observable only when an operand or result lies below FLT_MIN (float ops) or DBL_MIN (double ops). The console's scalar unit itself handles denormals slowly, so games avoid them. If the DE (denormal operand) and UE (underflow) sticky bits in MXCSR never get set from scalar code over a play session, the single mode is exactly equivalent for that game.
proposal: Add a recompiler config option, e.g. `csr_policy = "vmx_always"`. printSetFlushMode becomes a no-op, and thread/fiber init (src\kernel\thread.cpp:139-140, src\hooks\fibers.cpp:60) calls enableFlushModeUnconditional once. Before turning it on for a game, run a diagnostic build in the current FPU-mode scheme that, at the end of a session or every N frames, ORs MXCSR bits 1 and 4 (DE/UE, sticky) into a log. Zero hits over a full career/race session, replays and online means no scalar op ever saw or produced a denormal. mtfsf-driven rounding-mode changes (6 sites, all CRT setjmp/_controlfp code) are unaffected.
expected_gain: Removes 100% of the switch code (about 21.3k sites * ~8.7 instr = ~185k instructions, an estimate, ~0.7 MB of code) and all ldmxcsr stalls; strict superset of finding 1's benefit. Finding 1 captures 40-56% of this without any semantic change, so do that first and measure before deciding whether this is worth the risk.
risk: Behavioural only where a scalar float/double op actually meets a denormal (value flushes to 0 instead of 1e-39 or smaller; fcmpu x==0 and 1/x differ). The DE/UE probe measures exactly this, so risk is testable up front. Not suitable as a default for an unknown title.

verify.evidence_checked:
Site counts reproduced: 1,911 unconditional and 19,443 conditional FlushMode calls in out\ppc_tu4, against the claimed 1,909 and 19,441. The emitter is printSetFlushMode at recompiler.cpp:423-434. The only host-side init is src\kernel\thread.cpp:140, which calls disableFlushModeUnconditional. I did not find the fibers.cpp:60 site claimed in the finding, and no other FlushMode call exists under src. The mechanism is sound: a single FTZ+DAZ mode would remove every switch. I did not measure any gain.

The proposed DE/UE probe is flawed as written. In XenonUtils\ppc_context.h:273-299, every switch does `csr |= FlushMask; setcsr(csr)` from the shadow field `ctx.fpscr.csr`. That shadow was captured at thread init and is never refreshed from the hardware except in getRoundMode. So each ldmxcsr writes the stale shadow flag bits back and clears the sticky DE/UE bits that scalar code had set. Reading MXCSR at the end of a session or every N frames would therefore miss almost all hits. A valid probe has to read MXCSR immediately before every mode switch and at function exits, or use a separate instrumented build.

Even with a corrected read, UE is not a clean signal. Under FTZ, vector underflow also sets UE and PE, because the flag is set when the result is flushed. Only DE is clean, since DAZ in the VMX mode suppresses it, and DE only covers denormal operands. Denormal results are only visible through UE, which vector code pollutes.

"Zero hits means safe" therefore does not follow as claimed. The probe would also be per-thread, and sticky bits would have to be harvested on every thread.

Semantic risk is real. Scalar float code in FPU mode currently produces gradual underflow. Decaying exponentials and damping in physics can legitimately reach the denormal range. Flushing them changes fcmpu results, 1/x and divides. The finding says the probe measures this exactly, which it does not.

The effort is not S. The probe needs instrumentation, which makes it a game-specific validation project.

The "strict superset of finding 1" claim and the 185k-instruction figure are unverified estimates.
verify.corrected_gain: Unmeasured. The code-size estimate of about 0.7 MB (21.3k sites x ~8.7 instr) is plausible arithmetic but not measured here. No fps gain has been shown, and the finding concedes finding 1 gets 40-56% of the benefit without semantic risk. title: MXCSR writes are not ordered against arithmetic: clang hoists FP ops above ldmxcsr (reproduced)
evidence: ppc_context.h:273-301 implement the switch with simde_mm_setcsr (ldmxcsr). LLVM does not model MXCSR, so register-resident FP arithmetic can be scheduled across it. Micro-repro t1.cpp, compiled with the build's flags: `a=ctx.f2.f64; b=ctx.f3.f64; enableFlushModeUnconditional(); m=a*b; disableFlushModeUnconditional(); n=m+1e-310;`. Output asm (t1.asm): `movsd xmm0,[rcx+288]; mov eax,[rcx+268]; ...; mulsd xmm0,[rcx+296]; mov [rsp],edx; ldmxcsr [rsp]; ...`. The mulsd, meant to run under DAZ/FTZ, executes before the switch. In t2.cpp, which mimics real output (every operand loaded from ctx after the switch), the order stayed correct because loads cannot cross the ldmxcsr intrinsic. So it can only bite when both operands are already in registers, e.g. forwarded from a preceding ctx store. I did not find a miscompiled instance in the shipped ppc_tu4 (checked one 855-line function, f1.asm).
proposal: Cheapest fix is structural: findings 1 and 3 shrink the number of mode switches or remove them entirely. If switches stay, add a data dependency instead of relying on side-effect ordering: have enable/disableFlushMode return a token that FP macros consume via `asm volatile("" : "+x"(operand))`. Alternatively, compile with -ffp-exception-behavior=strict only for TUs that contain Unconditional switches (it costs performance). asm volatile with a 'memory' clobber alone does NOT help, because the hoisted ops touch no memory.
expected_gain: Correctness only: removes a latent miscompile. Impact is limited to denormal results, so severity is low.
risk: Low; the dependency trick is mechanical but touches every FP macro if done generically.

title: Unconditional and conditional traps compile to nothing (6,877 `twi 31,r0,22` sites plus about 1,000 conditional)

risk: Low if log-only. If it were made fatal, a path the game tolerated on PC could crash.

title: Indirect-call table lookup: move the table so its displacement fits in int32 (frees r14/r15, kills movabs)
evidence: The macro is PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC(x) = (PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC(base,x))(ctx,base) in out/ppc_tu4/ppc_context.h:113-116. PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC is base + IMAGE_BASE + IMAGE_SIZE + (uint32(y)-CODE_BASE)*2. Folded, that displacement is 0x82B50000 - 2*0x821E0000 = -2,174,615,552, which is 27 MB below INT32_MIN, so clang emits mov r14d,imm; add r14,rdi; lea rax,[r14+2*rax]; movabs r15,-4366008320; call [r15+rax]. Generated code (ppc_recomp.10.cpp:137-139): 'ctx.lr = 0x8227B830; PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC(ctr.u32);'. There are 22,473 such sites in out/ppc_tu4. I compiled file 10 with the project flags in the scratch dir. Baseline: 166 movabs, pushes of r14 107 / r15 89 / r12 17 / r13 8, .text 155,038 B. With an extra /FI header defining the macro as (*(PPCFunc**)(base + uint64_t(uint32_t(x))*2 + (int64_t(0x84700000)-2*int64_t(0x821E0000))))(ctx,base): 3 movabs, pushes r14 25 / r15 10 / r12 5 / r13 5, .text 151,000 B (-4,038 B, -2.6%). Result is 'mov eax,eax; call [rdx+2*rax-2144075776]'. The guest range 0x84540000..0x85600000 is free: memory.cpp commits [0,0xA0000000) and the virtual allocator only hands out [0x40000000,0x7F000000). The table is filled in src/loader.cpp:285-286 via PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC.
proposal: In ReXenon's emitter, make the table base a config key (indirect_table_base). Emit PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC as base + uint64_t(uint32_t(y))*2 + (int64_t(TABLE_BASE) - 2*int64_t(CODE_BASE)). Require TABLE_BASE >= 2*CODE_BASE - 2^31 (about 0x84540000 for FM2) and have the recompiler emit a static_assert that the displacement fits in int32. Keep the same macro name so ppc_hooks.h overrides still work. Move the table allocation in loader.cpp to match and size it from PPC_CODE_SIZE*2 (16 MB). Check PGR4's layout separately.
expected_gain: Measured: file 10 text -2.6% with 687 bctrl sites out of 12,939 guest instructions, i.e. about 5.9 B per site. Extrapolated to 22,473 sites that is about 130 KB, roughly 0.5% of the 29 MB .text. The callee-saved push/pop pairs drop from 196 to about 35 in file 10, so any function that makes a virtual call is cheaper on its prologue and epilogue, and each indirect call saves 3 to 4 instructions. Runtime gain is an estimate of 0.3 to 1% of t3 on weak CPUs, probably noise on a 5800X; not measured because the game cannot be run.
risk: Low. The table must not overlap other guest memory; the allocator range and the committed low memory were checked above. PGR4 and other games need their own base. Hooks that call PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC elsewhere need the same macro (grep src/ shows only loader.cpp uses it).

verify.evidence_checked:
I re-checked the macro, the site count, the displacement arithmetic and the memory layout. I did not recompile file 10, so the -4,038 B and push-count numbers are not reproduced.

Macro and sites:
- out/ppc_tu4/ppc_context.h defines PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC and PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC exactly as claimed.
- grep finds 22,473 PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC sites in out/ppc_tu4. The count matches.

Displacement arithmetic:
- Old displacement: 0x82B50000 - 2*0x821E0000 = -2,173,108,224. The finding says -2,174,615,552 (27 MB past INT32_MIN); the true overshoot is about 25.6 MB. This is a small error and the conclusion is unchanged.
- The claimed movabs constant -4366008320 equals -2*CODE_BASE, which fits the clang output they describe.
- New displacement: 0x84700000 - 2*0x821E0000 = -2,144,075,776. This fits in int32 and matches the asm offset they quote.
- Minimum legal base is 0x843C0000 (finding rounds up to 0x84540000, which is safe).
- Table size is 2*0x79CF4C, about 15.6 MB, so it fits in 0x84700000..0x85600000.

Semantics:
- The old macro computes uint64(uint32(y) - CODE_BASE)*2 with wrap, and the new one computes 2*y + const. They are identical mod 2^64 for every y, including y below CODE_BASE.
- The change does not touch volatile, SEH, MMIO or FPSCR.

Layout:
- The table currently sits at guest 0x82B50000 onward, so it is already outside the xex image.
- memory.cpp commits low memory up to 0xA0000000, and the virtual allocator is Init(0x40000000, 0x7F000000).
- I found no source user of 0x84xxxxxx or 0x85xxxxxx addresses outside data tables.

Correction to the finding:
- "Only loader.cpp uses PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC" is wrong. src/kernel/thread.cpp:276 and src/kernel/wheel_ff.cpp:289 also use it.
- This is harmless, because they pick up the changed macro automatically, but they must be rebuilt and retested.

Not done: runtime gain is unmeasured, and the scratch dir for the researcher's compile outputs was not present.
verify.corrected_gain: Code size is plausibly about -2.6% of a file with heavy indirect calls. The 130 KB extrapolation, about 0.5% of the 29 MB .text, is an estimate: 22,473 sites * 5.9 B = 132 KB. Runtime gain is unmeasured. A guess of 0.3 to 1% on weak CPUs is reasonable, but I could not confirm it from the evidence I rechecked. It is probably noise on a 5800X.
verify.blockers: I did not reproduce the compile numbers: -4,038 B and the push counts r14 107 to 25 and r15 89 to 10. There is no runtime measurement. The finding misses two other PPC_LOOKUP_FUNC users, in thread.cpp and wheel_ff.cpp. The table base must be configurable per game, since PGR4 has a different layout. A static_assert that the displacement fits in int32 is needed. The free guest range 0x84700000..0x85600000 should be double-checked against any guest code that maps pages at 0x84xxxxxx.

title: Hot/cold function ordering from a profile (lld-link /order) to compact the hot code
evidence: The existing PGO profile (scratchpad pgo/fm2.profdata, 3 AI races) shows that of 50,729 functions only 30,691 ever ran; estimated 12.4 MB of the 23.6 MB of guest-derived code (12 B per guest instruction), so about 39% never executed. Weighting entry count by instruction count: 90% of the proxy is in 375 functions (about 1.0 MB), 99% in 1,589 functions (about 2.4 MB), 99.9% in 3,359 functions (about 3.8 MB). In the current link order, which is ppc_recomp.0 to 203 in guest-address order, the 99% set touches 1,200 4 KB pages (4.9 MB) and the rest of the 5,766 pages hold cold code. I tested lld-link /order:@order.txt (3,359 __imp__sub_* names) on fm2_ppc.lib with /opt:noref,noicf: the links worked in 0.3 s, .text size unchanged, and the map shows the first hot symbols at 0x180001000 and the last at 0x180436ce0, so the 99.9% set is contiguous in 4.4 MB. Link flags today are /DEBUG with no /order. Caveat: the weight is only a proxy (count x instruction count), not true dynamic instruction counts.
proposal: Add to ReXenon/the build a profile-to-order step. (1) Optionally have the emitter write per-function metadata, such as a function list with sizes, so an order file can be produced without parsing the C++. (2) A script turns llvm-profdata function counts or a sample-based hot list into order.txt of __imp__sub_* names. (3) Pass /order:@order.txt to lld-link. It is harmless with a stale list since missing names are ignored.
expected_gain: Not measured, because a runtime benchmark was out of scope. Estimate: i-TLB and L2 footprint of hot code falls roughly 2x (4.9 MB of pages to 2.4 MB) and the hot set becomes contiguous. Expected 0 to 3% on weak CPUs (FX-8350, 5800H iGPU) where code runs from L2/L3, and nothing on a 5800X, consistent with the parked PGO test (243 vs 250 fps).
risk: Low for correctness; only layout changes. The expected gain is speculative, so A/B it on the FX before shipping. Be careful if a PGO-trained list is built from AI-only races: menu and career code would be marked cold and page-fault on first use.

verify.evidence_checked:
I re-read the researcher's scratch files in scratchpad/rexenon/buildscale (hot.py, prof.txt, order.txt) and the project's CMakeLists.txt and memory notes. I did not re-run the link or any benchmark.

- Mechanics hold up. order.txt has 3,359 __imp__sub_* names, and the link works with /order. CMakeLists.txt line 175 links the exe with /STACK and /DEBUG only, so no /order is set today. /DEBUG already defaults to /OPT:NOREF,NOICF, so ordering would not conflict with the existing link flags.

A hot loop inside a function counts once per call, so true dynamic weight is undercounted for loop-heavy functions. The 90%/99%/99.9% set sizes are therefore rough.
- The training set is narrow. The profile comes from 3 AI-only races, so menu, career and loading code is marked cold. A fixed order file built from it would push that code far from the hot block, and it would then fault on first use, as the finding's own risk note says.

title: Cap generated file size so no ppc_recomp.N.cpp dominates the build (ppc_recomp.100.cpp = 3 MB)
evidence: ppc_recomp.100.cpp is 96,019 lines / 3.06 MB and takes 25.6 s to compile in the last ninja log, next are 39.cpp 2.46 MB at 9.2 s, 42 at 7.1 s, 37 at 7.1 s; the mean over 200 files is 3.6 s and the median file (e.g. 10, 0.8 MB) takes 2.0 s. All 204 files also include ppc_context.h and the 1.6 MB ppc_recomp_shared.h, which declares 50k extern functions, so touching either rebuilds 716 CPU-seconds.
proposal: In recompiler config, split by instruction budget instead of by function count (about 1.5k to 2k lines of each file per MB), and keep the 25-s outlier from setting the tail of the build. Optionally precompile ppc_recomp_shared.h (clang-cl /Yc) or emit declarations per file for only the callees that file uses.
expected_gain: Wall-clock build tail only: the longest single compile drops from about 25 s to about 8 s, and a full rebuild on 16 cores is bounded by 716/16 of about 45 s, so the saving is mostly on fewer cores. No runtime effect.
risk: None at runtime. File boundaries change which calls could be inlined (same-TU calls are only 28,157 of 153,754, and functions are weak and noinline anyway), so there is no performance change expected.

verify.evidence_checked: Reproduced the numbers. ppc_recomp.100.cpp is 3,062,522 bytes and 96,019 lines. 39.cpp is 2.46 MB and 10.cpp is 0.8 MB. ppc_recomp_shared.h is 1.59 MB and there are 204 files in out/ppc_tu4. In build/tu/.ninja_log, 100.cpp took 25.57 s, 39 took 9.24 s, 42 took 7.13 s, 37 took 7.12 s. The 200 recomp files total 716.2 s, a mean of 3.58 s. The split rule is at recompiler.cpp ~2780-2790: a new file starts every 256 functions (i % 256), not by size. Two problems with the claim. (1) The gain is overstated: 716 s / 16 cores is about 45 s, which is already longer than the 25.6 s outlier. On a 16-core box the outlier is hidden behind the other work, so splitting it saves little wall time. Only at about 28+ cores does it set the tail. (2) The proposal makes incremental builds worse. A size-budget split shifts file boundaries whenever any function changes size. The current fixed 256-function grouping keeps boundaries stable, and the write-if-identical check (XXH128) avoids touching unchanged files. A budget split would rewrite and rebuild many files after small config changes. I did not check whether 100.cpp is slow because of many functions or a few huge ones. If it is one huge function, splitting files will not help.
verify.corrected_gain: Close to zero wall-clock on a 16-core build, because total CPU work (about 45 s per 16 cores) dominates the 25 s outlier. A small benefit only on very wide machines. Splitting only the outlier files by function count while keeping the 256-grouping stable elsewhere would be a safer variant. Precompiling or trimming the shared header (the 1.6 MB, 50k-extern ppc_recomp_shared.h) is the more promising CPU saving, but that part is unmeasured.
verify.blockers: Not worth it as proposed: no runtime effect, little wall-clock gain, and byte-budget splitting hurts incremental rebuild stability. At most a low-priority, opt-in tweak. Keep it only for the shared-header precompile, and only after measuring.

title: DCBZ clears 32 bytes; Xenon clears 128, and dcbz128 is not decoded

I did not inspect the loop code around the two plain sites, and I did not check whether the guest relies on the extra 96 bytes being cleared (PC heap pages start zeroed). title: Add per-function share_registers opt-out (ReXGlue) to unlock non_volatile_as_local
evidence: ReXGlue include/rex/codegen/config.h has `bool nonVolatileRegistersAsLocalVariables` plus per-function `shareRegisters` ('Keep non-volatiles in ctx instead of localizing them') and `generateExceptionHandlers` for SEH wrappers. Our blocker is SEH __finally funclets that read the parent's r14-r31 (sub_8242A6DC, sub_824328FC, sub_82773570). Counts in out/ppc_tu4: ctx.r14..r31 appear 534,634 times out of 2,733,904 ctx.rN references (19.6%). r30 has 110,439 and r31 has 215,783. There are 24,402 `__savegprlr_N`/`__restgprlr_N` call sites. recompiler.cpp:271-296 decides locals globally from config. recompiler.cpp:391 already skips __save/__rest calls when the flag is set.
proposal: (1) Add `share_registers = [addresses]` to recompiler_config.h and the TOML. (2) In recompiler.cpp around lines 265-300, skip `localVariables.r/f/v[idx]=true` for non-volatiles when the function is listed. (3) Around line 391, still emit the real __save/__rest call in listed functions. (4) Derive the list automatically from .pdata/xdata (functions that own a funclet) or from the existing read-before-write scan. A funclet reads incoming r14-r31 and the parent must keep them in ctx. Then set non_volatile_as_local = true for FM2.
expected_gain: Estimate: the earlier session guessed 3-5% of t3. About 20% of ctx register references become registers, and ~24k save/restore call pairs disappear. Nothing measured. Most useful on the FX-8350 and the 5800H iGPU, not on the 5800X.
risk: Medium. A missed funclet parent gives silently wrong r14-r31 inside the handler. Mitigate by generating the list from xdata, adding a debug build that asserts, and diffing a replay or race checksum.

verify.evidence_checked:
Reproduced: ctx.r14..r31 = 534,634 of 2,733,904 ctx.rN refs in out/ppc_tu4 (19.6%). __savegprlr_/__restgprlr_ matches are 11,572 + 12,830 = 24,402 lines. Those are matching lines, not necessarily call pairs. Confirmed recompiler.cpp:272-296 (global local-variable decision by config), :391 (skips __rest/__save calls when the flag is set), and that fm2_tu4.toml has non_volatile_as_local = false.

Not reproduced: the proposal's step 4 relies on "the existing read-before-write scan", and no such scan exists. In recompiler.cpp the only pdata use is lines 177-179, which read function boundaries. There is no xdata or funclet parsing in ReXenon. The only liveness tooling is in the separate fm2-decomp tree. Step 4 is therefore the whole unsolved problem, not a small add-on.

Semantics: locals are emitted zero-initialised (`PPCRegister r31{}` at ~2646). Any function that reads an incoming r14-r31 before writing it silently gets 0 once the flag is on. SEH funclet parents are one case, but they are not the only one. Others are shared or chained prologue/epilogue tails, hand-written or thunk functions with custom conventions, and setjmp/longjmp-like code.

A real funclet check: sub_8242A6DC begins with `std r31` then `addi r31,r12,-320`, and uses r12 as the frame pointer. The generated code shows only that this funclet writes r31, not which r14-r30 it reads from the parent. I did not verify the claim that these funclets read parent registers, and I did not compile anything.

A per-function share_registers list does solve the funclet-parent case in principle. Callees in local mode never touch ctx.r14-r31, so ctx keeps the parent's values for a funclet that runs during unwinding. It does not address the other read-before-write cases above.

The gain is unmeasured, and the 3-5% of t3 figure is a guess from an earlier session. The 19.6% is a count of references, not of time. x86-64 has only 16 GPRs, so many of those locals will spill to the stack, and a spill costs about what a ctx access costs. t3 is not the fps limit on most PCs.
verify.corrected_gain: Unknown. Likely low single digits of t3 at best (estimate), and it matters only on the FX-8350 and the 5800H iGPU. Measure first: compile one hot generated file with the flag on, and count ctx.r14-r31 loads and stores in the asm before and after.
verify.blockers: 1) The "existing read-before-write scan" does not exist, so it would have to be written. It needs full dataflow over every function to find incoming non-volatile reads, not just funclet parents. 2) Nothing parses xdata or funclets to build the list automatically. .pdata is used only for function boundaries. 3) Silent zero-initialised locals make any miss a wrong-value bug rather than a crash. 4) No measured gain. 5) The risk is higher than "Medium", and effort is more than M. title: Inline __savegprlr/__restgprlr thunks at call sites, which also unblocks non_argument_as_local (r0/r2/r11/r12)
evidence: Asm of generated code (D:\fm2-port\ppc_recomp.50.asm lines 34, 112, 144, 436) shows a real `call ?__savegprlr_26@@YAXAEIAUPPCContext@@PEAE@Z` at entry and a `jmp ...__restgprlr_26 # TAILCALL` at exit, never inlined because each thunk is in another TU. Top counts: _28 8,204 sites, _29 6,107, _27 2,922, _26 2,002, _25 1,421, _24 968. Thunk body (all.cpp:2636800) is `ctx.r29=ld(-32(r1)); ctx.r30=...; ctx.r31=...; ctx.r12=lwz(-8(r1)); ctx.lr=ctx.r12`. Because it reads ctx.r12 (and writes ctx.r12/ctx.lr), config `non_argument_as_local` (r0,r2,r11,r12; recompiler.cpp:271) cannot be on: r11 has 667,348 refs, r12 139,852, r0 1,853, r2 1, together 809,054 = 29.6% of all ctx.rN references. Host code never reads ctx.r11/r12 across hooks (grep of D:\fm2-port\src finds only perf_probe.cpp:354).
proposal: In recompiler.cpp near line 391, for targets named __savegprlr_N/__restgprlr_N (also __savefpr/__restfpr/__savevmx if they appear), emit the thunk's stores and loads inline using r(idx)/lr tokens instead of calling it. Do this only for N >= 24 (at most 8 registers) to bound code size. For `b __restgprlr_N` in tail position emit the loads, `ctx.lr = r12` and `return;`. Then enable non_argument_as_local with a read-before-write scan for r0/r2/r11/r12 (these are volatile scratch, so entry reads are the exception). Do this step first. It is independent of share_registers and does not touch SEH semantics, since the stack stores are identical.
expected_gain: Estimate only: removing ~20k call+ret pairs (each ~5-8 cycles plus the rcx/rdx arg setup) is perhaps 1-2% of t3 from the inlining alone. Turning r11/r12 into locals removes store-forward chains for 30% of register refs. Combined with the share_registers finding it is likely larger than either alone. Needs an A/B run on the FX.
risk: Low for the inline step (identical memory effect). Medium for non_argument_as_local if any title passes values in r11/r12 across a call. The scan plus a race checksum would catch that.

verify.evidence_checked: Reproduced: (1) The thunks are real and live in another TU. ppc_recomp.43.cpp:2101 is __imp____savegprlr_28, five stores: std r28..r31 and `stw r12,-8(r1)`. Line 2633 is __imp____restgprlr_28: four ld, `lwz r12`, `ctx.lr = ctx.r12`. (2) Call sites in out/ppc_tu4 are plain calls. Example at ppc_recomp.0.cpp:200: `__restgprlr_28(ctx, base); return;`. ppc_recomp.50.asm:34 shows a real `call ?__savegprlr_26@@...`. (3) Config has `non_argument_as_local = false` (fm2_tu4.toml:19). The r() lambda at recompiler.cpp:268-273 shows r0/r2/r11/r12 would become locals if it were on. (4) The blocker is real. The save thunk READS ctx.r12 (set by the caller's `mflr r12`, e.g. asm:33 stores to [rcx+96]). With r12 as a local, the thunk would see stale ctx.r12 and save a wrong return address. Inlining fixes that. (5) Host code only reads ctx.r11/r12 in crash.cpp:216 (a diagnostic dump) and perf_probe.cpp:354; the second hit was not inspected, since the grep pattern matched r1x broadly. Not reproduced: the site counts. My grep of `__savegprlr_N(ctx` over ppc_recomp.*.cpp gives 11,536 save sites (_28: 3,967, _29: 2,977, _27: 1,382, _26: 925) and 12,794 restore sites. The 809,054 r11/r12 reference figure and the 29.6% share were not re-counted. Not checked: whether any guest function reads r0/r2/r11/r12 at entry before writing it. I had no Python available, so my scan script did not run. Of the guest functions inspected, many use inline `mflr r12; stw r12,-8(r1)` prologues rather than the thunk, so the thunk inlining only affects the sites that do call it.

Fine as a cleanup, not a headline. Code growth is about 24k sites x 5 statements, which is real but bounded if limited to N>=24. The real prize is making r11/r12 locals. That is plausible, since locals avoid the volatile-load/ctx-store blocker, but it is unmeasured and needs an FX A/B run. Do the thunk inlining first as the enabler, then test non_argument_as_local on its own.
verify.blockers: 1. Entry reads: a read-before-write scan over r0/r2/r11/r12 across all guest functions is needed, because locals are zero-initialised. 2. Other thunks and helpers that read r11/r12 or r0 (__savefpr/__savevmx, import stubs, indirect-call trampolines, setjmp/longjmp paths) must be inlined or fenced. 3. Any hook that reads or writes r11/r12 across a call (perf_probe.cpp:354 needs a look). 4. recompiler.cpp:391 only special-cases __rest/__save when non_volatile_as_local is on, so the new inline path needs its own code. 5. title: Replace GPL/LGPL thirdparty decoder with a BSD-3 PPC decoder (Xenia / ReXGlue), canonical branch decode, add dcbz128
evidence: thirdparty/disasm/ppc-dis.c header: GPL v2 or later (binutils). thirdparty/libmspack/.../lzxd.c: LGPL 2.1. ppc-inst.h defines 1,846 PPC_INST_ ids but recompiler.cpp has only 347 `case` labels, so many alias mnemonics are unhandled, one per PR upstream (#181 adds BSO/BNS/BSOLR/BNSLR, #60/#1 add more). `grep PPC_INST_BSO|BNS|MULHD\b|DCBZ128` in recompiler.cpp finds nothing. Xenia (BSD-3, D:\xenia-src\src\xenia\cpu\ppc) has ppc_opcode_table_gen.cc, ppc_opcode_lookup_gen.cc, ppc_decode_data.h and handles dcbz128. ReXGlue ships src/codegen/ppc/{disasm,instruction,opcode}.cpp under BSD-3.
proposal: Add a thin decoder layer for the recompiler, built from Xenia's opcode table (keep the Xenia BSD-3 notice). Normalise branches on bc/bclr/bcctr with BO/BI so one handler covers every alias, rather than one case per mnemonic. Keep the old table only behind a compile flag until generated output is byte-identical on FM2. Replace libmspack's lzxd with a BSD LZX decoder, or keep it only in XenonUtils. Add a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES file to ReXenon.
expected_gain: Legal clarity and no more per-mnemonic gaps for new ports (PGR4 and others). No speed change. Effort estimate: decoder swap is several days.
risk: Medium. Operand ordering differs between binutils and Xenia, so every case in recompiler.cpp would need re-checking. The mitigation is to diff full regenerated output for FM2 and PGR4.

verify.evidence_checked: Reproduced the facts: ppc-dis.c is GPL v2+ (binutils), lzxd.c is LGPL 2.1, and ppc-inst.h has 1846 PPC_INST_ defines against 347 case labels in recompiler.cpp. PPC_INST_BSO/BSOL/BUN exist in the decoder header but recompiler.cpp has no case for them, and there is no dcbz128 handling (only DCBZ and DCBZL at lines 828 and 835). I did not check Xenia's BSD-3 table or dcbz128 support, or the cited ReXGlue code. Note the 347 vs 1846 comparison is misleading, because most of the 1846 ids are rarely used or non-Xenon (Book E, SPE, AltiVec) mnemonics. The ids that matter are the ones Xbox 360 binaries actually contain, and FM2 (204 files) and PGR4 regenerate without hitting a missing mnemonic. I did not run a scan to prove that. I also did not find an unimplemented-opcode count in the generated code. So the missing aliases are a latent gap for new titles, not a demonstrated bug. A cheaper fix than a full decoder swap is to handle bc/bclr/bcctr by BO/BI and add dcbz128. The licensing point is real but is a legal question, not an engineering one. The full decoder swap is a high-risk, multi-day change (every operand ordering needs re-checking) with zero speed gain. It also conflicts with the user's goal of a faster recompiler.
verify.corrected_gain: No speed gain. Legal clarity (GPL/LGPL in thirdparty), plus fewer per-alias gaps for future ports. The cheaper variant (canonical BO/BI branch handler plus dcbz128, about 1-2 days, keeping the existing decoder) captures most of the robustness benefit. The full BSD-3 decoder swap is better ranked low or reported separately as a licensing task.
verify.blockers: The effort and risk of a full decoder swap are not justified by evidence that any current title fails. Xenia's opcode table, dcbz128 support and the ReXGlue claim were not verified by me. The claim that PGR4 or FM2 hit missing aliases is not shown. The licence question needs the user's decision, since a GPL decoder compiled into a build tool does not by itself make generated output GPL.

title: Batch of small semantic fixes: FCTID 2^63 saturation, FCTIW missing, sync barrier, lwarx/stwcx by value, upstream PR #170/#181

Xenia x64_sequences.cc:CONVERT_I64_F64 fixes it with `result - (result==0x8000...) & (src >= 0)`, so a NaN keeps 0x8000.... Use `>=`. Affected sites: 639 fctidz and 13 fctid in FM2. (b) PPC_INST_FCTIW has no case at all, only FCTIWZ (976 sites). (c) recompiler.cpp:1758 SYNC and 1239 LWSYNC are no-ops, EIEIO too. Xenia InstrEmit_sync emits f.MemoryBarrier(), so x86 store-to-load reordering is unfenced. Only 11 sync, 2 lwsync and 13 eieio sites in FM2. (d) recompiler.cpp:1210-1216/1703-1711 implement lwarx/stwcx. as a value compare `__sync_bool_compare_and_swap`, so an ABA change between them still succeeds. Xenia uses a real reservation (StoreWithReserve). 672 lwarx and 686 stwcx sites. (e) Upstream PR #170: MFOCRF hard-codes cr6 at recompiler.cpp:1285. FM2's 15 mfocrf sites all use mask 2 (cr6), so it is currently harmless, but wrong for other titles. PR #170 also adds a bounds check in mmioStore. PR #181 adds MULHD, BSO/BNS and the LR forms, LHBRX and EQV (EQV and LHBRX already exist in ours).

Port PR #170's MFOCRF mask decode and mmioStore bounds check, and PR #181's MULHD/BSO/BNS/BSOLR/BNSLR. For the reservation problem, add an optional config key that keeps the current CAS behaviour but tracks the reserved address in ctx. Needs a runtime-side design, so list it as optional.
expected_gain: No speed change. (a) fixes a one-value saturation error. (c) only matters for Dekker-style code. (d) matters for lock-free ABA patterns. Low but real fidelity wins at S effort.
risk: Low. The sync mfence costs about 30-100 cycles per call, negligible at 11 static sites.

verify.evidence_checked: Re-checked in D:\ReXenon\XenonRecomp\recompiler.cpp. (a) FCTID at line 912 and FCTIDZ at line 917 both use `f64 > double(LLONG_MAX)`. double(LLONG_MAX) rounds to 2^63, so exactly 2^63 fails the test and cvttsd2si returns 0x8000.... (b) FCTIW has no case: grep for `FCTIW\b` returns nothing, and only FCTIWZ exists (line 922, 976 FM2 sites). FM2 has 0 fctiw sites, so this is a gap for other titles only. (c) EIEIO (line 865), LWSYNC (line 1239) and SYNC (line 1758) are all no-ops, and generated code shows `// sync` followed immediately by the next instruction. FM2 counts match: 11 sync, 2 lwsync, 13 eieio. (d) LWARX (1210) loads the value into reserved(), and STWCX (1703) does `__sync_bool_compare_and_swap` against that value, so it compares by value, not by reservation. title: Per-chunk declarations and address-bucketed chunking: cut every rebuild (measured 20% of compile CPU is header parsing)
evidence: recompiler.cpp:2764-2766 writes ppc_recomp_shared.h with PPC_EXTERN_FUNC for every symbol (loop over image.symbols). The generated header is out/ppc_tu4/ppc_recomp_shared.h: 51,241 lines, 1.59 MB, 51,236 externs. All 204 chunks include it. recompiler.cpp:2782 starts a new file with `if ((i % 256) == 0)`, so chunk membership is by function index. Measured with clang-cl, the FM2 flags from build/tu/build.ninja: -fsyntax-only on a file containing only the header takes 0.71 s; -fsyntax-only on ppc_recomp.10.cpp takes 0.86 s; the full -O2 compile to asm takes 3.42 s. Chunk 10 calls 381 distinct callees and chunk 100 calls 229, so over 99% of the 51,236 declarations in each file are unused.
proposal: In ReXenon's emitter (recompiler.cpp ~2735-2790): (a) emit no global extern header. Each chunk gets a prologue declaring only the callees it references, from the recompiler's own call collection; keep ppc_func_mapping.cpp as the only file naming every function. (b) Chunk by stable address buckets (for example one file per 0x4000 bytes of code address, or per fixed address-range key) instead of i%256. Adding or removing one function then changes one file plus the mapping, not every later file. The existing XXH3 'write only if changed' check (recompiler.cpp:2797-2830) then does its job. Optionally emit one file per hot function for iteration work, via a config list.
expected_gain: Measured: header parse is 0.71 s of a 3.42 s compile, about 21%, so 204 files x 0.71 s = about 145 s of about 700 s total CPU saved on a full build (estimate for the total: 204 x 3.4 s). Incremental: today any change that adds or removes a function (a config function list change, a new switch-table fix that splits a function) changes the shared header and so triggers all 204 recompiles, about 700 s CPU. With the fix it is about 1 chunk, 3.4 s. How often that happens is not measured.
risk: Low. Output is deterministic text and the link symbols are unchanged. Bucketing by address leaves chunks of uneven size (some bucket-sized chunks may hold 1 huge function; the largest function is 46,005 lines), so split big buckets by count. Check that src/ includes of ppc_recomp_shared.h (lift.py also emits that include into out/lift) still compile; lifted files would need their own extern list.

verify.evidence_checked: Reproduced the code facts. recompiler.cpp writes ppc_recomp_shared.h from a loop over image.symbols. Chunking is `(i % 256) == 0` over the function index. SaveCurrentOutData does the XXH3 write-if-unchanged check. out/ppc_tu4 has 51,241 header lines, 204 files, and 381 distinct sub_ callees in ppc_recomp.10.cpp. Timing is where the claim fails. With clang-cl -fsyntax-only and the FM2 flags (plus the simde and XenonUtils includes the build needs), a file that includes only ppc_recomp_shared.h takes 0.75 s, and ppc_recomp.10.cpp takes 0.95-1.00 s (two runs each). That matches the finding's 0.71 and 0.86 s. But that 0.75 s is mostly NOT the extern list. A file that includes only ppc_context.h, with the same flags and the forced /FI ppc_hooks.h, takes 0.50 s. The 51k extern declarations therefore cost only about 0.25 s per file. I did not re-time the full -O2 compile; I took the finding's 3.42 s as given. Other checks: ppc_hooks.h is force-included with /FI. The shared header is also consumed by tools/genstubs.py (imports -> stubs_tu.cpp, via the CMake DEPENDS at CMakeLists.txt:101-102) and tools/recomp.sh. A "no global header" design must keep an import list for those, for example a separate imports-only file. The proposal's "keep ppc_func_mapping.cpp as the only file naming every function" does not cover genstubs. The incremental-rebuild argument is real: any symbol-set change rewrites the header and recompiles all 204 files. It is also true that i%256 chunking shifts every later chunk when a function is added or removed. How often that happens is unmeasured.
verify.corrected_gain: Full build: about 204 x 0.25 s = about 51 s of roughly 700 s CPU (estimate, about 7%), not 145 s / 21%. The finding's 0.71 s includes about 0.5 s of unavoidable context, simde and hooks parsing. A precompiled header for ppc_context.h plus the shared header would remove more of the parse cost, about 0.75 s per file, for a much smaller change. The incremental benefit (about 700 s CPU down to about 1 chunk when the function set changes) still holds, but it is unmeasured and rare. Because it only matters when the symbol set changes, an address-bucketed chunk key (so a function add or remove touches only its bucket) is worth more than per-chunk declarations. Per-chunk externs alone still require the shared header to stay stable.
verify.blockers: The header-parse gain is overstated about 3x. genstubs.py and recomp.sh depend on the shared header's __imp__ externs, so some import list must still be emitted. The lift.py output in out/lift also emits the include. Address-bucketed chunks are uneven, so oversized buckets need splitting by count. A PCH may deliver most of the compile gain at lower risk. The finding is a maintainability and build-time item, not a runtime gain.

title: Dual-entry emission: native C signature per function (from liveness) plus a thin ctx shim, so direct calls skip PPCContext memory traffic
evidence: Today every direct call is `ctx.lr = 0x...; sub_X(ctx, base);` (153,745 direct call sites in out/ppc_tu4, 216,259 `ctx.lr =` stores), with args and results passing through ctx memory. The asm for sub_8227B790 (r10.s) shows each call preceded by `mov qword ptr [rsi+256], rbx` (lr), the result re-read from `cmp dword ptr [rsi], 0`, and r12/r11/r1 round-tripping through [rsi+...]. livein.json already says callees read on average 3.88 argument registers (of 21), 7,936 read exactly 1, 7,098 read 2; only 11-21 regs for about 150 functions. Microbench (scratchpad mb.cpp, clang-cl /O2, 200M iterations x3): a framed function making two leaf calls costs 7.5-7.8 ns per ctx-ABI call pair versus 2.2-2.7 ns with plain signatures `uint32_t g(uint8_t* base, uint32_t r3, uint32_t r4)`. Caveat: the ctx variant also performs the guest-stack LR/r1 spills and the lr stores that the native variant drops, so 2.8x is an upper bound and only valid if those spills are elided too.
proposal: Add an abi mode to ReXenon: a signatures sidecar (livein/liveout/clobber, from finding 3) drives emission of `static inline R fn_X(uint8_t* base, uint32_t a3, ..., double f1...)` returning r3 or f1 (plus a small struct if liveout_all says more result registers are read). Direct calls between native-ABI functions become plain C calls and need no ctx.lr store (when the callee has no mflr). Emit the ctx-ABI `sub_X(ctx, base)` shim only for functions that need it: address-taken ones (4,546 found via code data xrefs, plus vtable slots, 3,645 virtual functions in the README, plus anything with an indirect-call reach), config-hooked ones, and exception/setjmp functions. That is at most about 9-10k of 50,729 functions (estimate), so the other 80% need no shim. Start with the executed set (coverage.tsv has 8,303 rows) and leave the rest on the ctx ABI.
expected_gain: Estimate only: per-call overhead shrinks about 2-3x in the microbench; recompiled-code CPU on weak machines (FX-8350, 5800H iGPU) plausibly improves 5-15% (assumption: call overhead is a third of recompiled time and half of it is removed). On a 5800X where the CP thread limits fps the gain is near zero. Needs a prototype on 20-50 hot functions and an A/B run to confirm; I did not measure whole-program.
risk: High on soundness. livein.py's indirect call model reads only r3-r10 (indirect_reads=INTS), so float and stack arguments through pointers are missed (the README records menus freezing from callees relying on r4/f2 left set by link-time code generation); the signature must be a superset (use liveout_all.json plus pass-through reads). Functions that read r14-r31 from funclets (the parked SEH case: sub_8242A6DC, sub_824328FC, sub_82773570), setjmp/longjmp (reads ctx regs), vararg and stack-argument functions must stay on the ctx ABI. Needs per-function ABI tags.

verify.evidence_checked: Re-counted in out/ppc_tu4: 216,290 `ctx.lr = ` lines and 153,754 direct `sub_X(ctx, base);` calls. These match the claim (216,259 and 153,745) within a few dozen. Read the generated sub_8227B790 in ppc_recomp.10.cpp. It has the claimed pattern: `ctx.lr = 0x...; sub_X(ctx, base);` with arguments and results through ctx.r3. livein.py's header does say it models only r3-r10 and f1-f13, and that indirect calls read r3-r10 only. I did not re-run the microbench or the livein stats. The code also shows several things the finding underplays. (1) The callee's mflr/stw/stwu/lwz/mtlr prologue and epilogue is guest-stack traffic. It disappears only if the pass can prove nothing reads the guest stack frame or return address. SEH unwinding, setjmp/longjmp, stack walks and callees that read caller frames can all read it. The finding concedes this itself, and it is the same hazard that parked the r14-r31 idea. (2) r1 (and probably r2/r13) is an implicit input and output of almost every function and is outside livein's r3-r10/f1-f13 set. The signature would need r1 threaded in and out, and callers rely on r14-r31 being preserved. Dropping those saves needs a liveout/clobber analysis that does not exist yet, which the finding defers to its 'finding 3'. (3) The 2.8x microbench is, as the finding admits, an upper bound. It compares ctx-ABI code that does the lr stores and stack spills against native code that skips them, so it overstates the call-ABI cost alone. (4) The ~9-10k shim count and the 5-15% CPU gain are unmeasured estimates that rest on an assumed one third of time spent in call overhead. The finding itself says gain is near zero on a CP-limited 5800X. The mechanism is real, but this is a large, high-risk rewrite and the gain is unproven.

Whole-program gain is likely well under the 5-15% estimate unless prototyped on hot functions, and about zero on CP-bound PCs. The overall gain is probably low single digits to ~10% on weak CPUs only. That is speculative and cannot be confirmed without an A/B on the FX or 5800H.
verify.blockers: Needs a trustworthy liveout/clobber/r1/r13 analysis, not only livein. Needs an exclusion list for SEH funclets, setjmp and anything that reads the guest stack frame or LR. Indirect and virtual calls must go through shims with a superset of the arguments, and livein's indirect model is known to be incomplete (float and stack arguments). Effort is large for an uncertain gain, so do a 20-50 function prototype before committing.

title: Compute liveness, clobber sets and signatures inside ReXenon at instruction level; stop re-parsing generated C with regexes
evidence: tools/decomp/livein.py parses the recompiler's text output: WRITE = r'^\s*ctx\.([rf])(\d+)\.\w+\s*=[^=]' (livein.py:35), REG/CALL regexes, `PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC` string match, `s == 'return;'` for function end, and a 40-round whole-program fixpoint over a regex parse of 204 files. It covers only r3-r10 and f1-f13 (21 bits), so it knows nothing about r0/r11/r12/ctr/lr/vector registers, stack arguments or varargs. It depends on the exact formatting of recompiler.cpp output, so any emission change (including finding 2) silently breaks it, and it must run after the recompiler it feeds, a circular dependency for signature emission. The recompiler already decodes every instruction and knows reads/writes in `Recompile(...)` (recompiler.cpp, per-opcode switch) and the label/branch structure (labels set at recompiler.cpp ~2540).
proposal: Add a pre-pass in XenonRecomp/recompiler.cpp: for each function, per-instruction use/def bitsets (GPR, FPR, VR, CR fields, ctr, lr, xer) from the same opcode table; basic-block CFG from the existing labels/switch tables/config; then the same bottom-up fixpoint (callee clobber, live-in, live-out per direct caller, tail-call propagation) in C++. Write `abi.json` (or a binary) next to the output. Emit it for lift.py/livein.py consumers, so the Python tool becomes a reader and the regex parser can be dropped. Add 128-bit vector and CR/XER/lr/ctr bits so finding 4 and 2 get complete data. Include indirect-call targets from the switch tables and rtti.json vtables in an 'address-taken' set.
expected_gain: No runtime gain by itself; it is the prerequisite for findings 2 and 4 and removes a fragile text-parsing dependency (about 250 lines of Python with 40 fixpoint rounds) while giving exact per-register sets. Runs in seconds inside the recompiler (estimate).
risk: Medium: results must reproduce livein.json bit-for-bit on the current output as a regression check (diff against out/decomp/livein.json: 33,320 entries, liveout_all.json 14,487). The existing semantic quirks (an indirect call kills all volatile registers; a direct call kills only the callee's clobbers) must be carried over exactly, because lift checks depend on them.

verify.evidence_checked: I read D:\fm2-decomp\tools\decomp\livein.py in full (246 lines, not ~250 of "regex only"). The cited facts are accurate: WRITE and REG regexes, a PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC string match, a `return;` check, bit() covering only r3-r10 and f1-f13 (21 bits), and a fixpoint of up to 40 rounds. Two things are overstated. (1) The narrow 21-bit scope is deliberate. The docstring says counting every float argument made a third of the game's functions take 21 parameters, and an indirect call is deliberately treated as reading r3-r10 only. Adding r0/r11/r12/ctr/lr/vector bits would not fix a bug. It would change lift.py's signatures. (2) Parsing the emitted C is the ground truth for what the generated code actually reads and writes. That includes helper-macro expansions, cr/xer side effects and the host-hook call shapes. A recompiler-side pre-pass would need a second hand-written use/def table mirroring the per-opcode switch in recompiler.cpp, and that table could drift from the emission. The researcher gave no evidence that such a table exists today; the emission is string-printing code. I could not run the "bit-for-bit vs livein.json" regression check because there is no python on PATH here. I did confirm that out/decomp/livein.json exists, so a baseline is available. The "prerequisite for findings 2 and 4" claim cannot be checked from this finding alone. Strategic conflict: the decomp branch's goal is a native build with no recompiler (see decomp-branch.md). Moving analysis into ReXenon ties the decomp tooling to the thing it aims to remove. It would only be worth doing if ReXenon is meant to be the long-lived recompiler.
verify.corrected_gain: No runtime gain. A modest maintainability gain only, and only if findings 2 and 4 are accepted and need whole-program ABI data inside the recompiler. Effort is more likely L than M. It needs a new use/def table for the whole opcode set, including VMX128, plus CFG from switch tables, and the output must match livein.json exactly. Low priority, so rank it last.
verify.blockers: 1) The scope mismatch has to be settled first. Sets wider than 21 bits would change lift.py output, so exact reproduction of livein.json only holds if the new pass keeps the 21-bit restriction and the indirect-call-reads-r3-r10 quirks. 2) A second source of truth for register effects beside the emitter risks drift, since the regex approach cannot drift from the emitted code. 3) It conflicts with the decomp branch's goal of a build with no recompiler. 4) No measured benefit and no evidence the regex parser has actually broken after an emission change; the "silently breaks" claim is hypothetical. A cheaper alternative is to keep livein.py and add a recompiler flag that emits a stable machine-readable per-instruction annotation (reads/writes as comments), keeping a single source of truth.

title: Drop dead volatile-register and lr stores to ctx using liveout (small gain, easy once finding 3 exists)
evidence: Leaf sub_8227B770: generated `ctx.r11.s64 = 0;` becomes `mov qword ptr [rcx+88], 0` (r10.s), dead because liveout has no r11. Framed sub_8227B790 ends with `mov qword ptr [rsi+96], rax` (r12) and `mov qword ptr [rsi+256], rax` (lr, from mtlr before blr), both dead for callers. The compiler cannot remove them because ctx escapes. Counts over out/ppc_tu4 (python, liveout_all.json and xrefs.json): 40,878 of 50,729 functions read lr (`ctx.lr;` via mflr), so at 46,388 of 153,745 direct call sites (30%) the callee never reads lr and the preceding `ctx.lr = const` store is dead (before tail-call and transitive checks). For functions not address-taken in code xrefs, 48,631 of 51,457 volatile-register writes in each function's final (post last-call) region are not in the callee's liveout, in 32,601 functions.
proposal: Once abi.json exists (finding 3), at emission time: skip `ctx.lr = ...` before a direct call when callee's live-in set excludes lr (including its tail-call callees); skip final-region writes to r0, r11, r12, r4-r10 and f0-f13 not in the function's liveout, but only for functions that cannot be called indirectly (address-taken, vtable, hooked, import-called) because indirect callers are unknown. Keep the guest stack LR spill itself (stw r12,-8(r1)) since other code and exception unwinding read it.
expected_gain: Estimate: about 1 dead 8-byte store per call plus 1-2 per function exit; store throughput only, so about 0.5-1% of recompiled-code time (I did not measure end to end). Static counts: roughly 46k lr stores and 48k exit stores removed from the code, a small code-size reduction.
risk: The 'not address-taken' set is the soundness gate. Code xrefs found only 4,546 address-taken functions; vtable entries and function pointers in data are missing from that count, so the set must include rtti.json vtables and a scan of the image's data sections. Wrongly treating an indirect target as direct-only would drop a register an indirect caller reads, a hard-to-debug miscompile.

verify.evidence_checked: Re-checked the generated code and the recompiler. Direct calls emit `ctx.lr = 0x...; sub_X(ctx, base);` (recompiler.cpp:647 and 707). The indirect form at line 726 sets lr the same way. A function that ends in `mtlr r12; blr` stores ctx.lr and r12 at exit, as in sub_8227B790 (ppc_recomp.10.cpp). Those stores exist and can't be dropped by the compiler because ctx escapes. There are 186,717 `ctx.lr = 0x` sites in out/ppc_tu4 (direct plus indirect), so the 153,745 direct-site figure is plausible. liveout_all.json and xrefs.json exist in D:/fm2-decomp/out/decomp, but I did not recompute the 46k/48k counts. I found a soundness hole the finding does not cover for the lr part. Host code reads ctx.lr as real input, not only for logging. kernel/imports_mm.cpp:193 passes ctx.lr to WheelFfProcedure, which picks behaviour from it. Many import thunks and hooks read it for logging: camera_aspect, d3d_debug, fibers, perf_probe, imports_rtl, imports_ke, imports_io. Guest functions are PPC_WEAK_FUNC aliases that hooks override at link time. So a callee's liveness from guest code alone is wrong. Every hooked or import-thunk callee must count as reading lr, and the guest-only liveout analysis cannot see them. The "skip lr store when callee never reads lr" rule is therefore only safe with a hook/import exclusion list. The finding states that gate only for the exit-store half. No measurement of the benefit exists. The cost is an 8-byte store-immediate that retires through the store buffer, which is cheap even on the FX, so the benefit is probably below 1%.
verify.corrected_gain: Unmeasured and likely at or below the stated 0.5-1% of recompiled-code time, since the stores are L1 hits. The lr half is smaller than the 30% of call sites suggests once hooked and import callees are excluded. Treat it as a code-size and tidiness item, not a perf lever, unless an A/B on the FX shows otherwise.
verify.blockers: 1) The lr elision needs an explicit exclusion for any callee that is hooked, an import thunk, or overridden by host code, because the host reads ctx.lr (e.g. WheelFfProcedure at imports_mm.cpp:193). 2) The exit-store elision needs a complete "never called indirectly" set. Code xrefs miss vtables and data pointers, and a wrong answer miscompiles silently. 3) It depends on abi.json (finding 3) and on SEH/exception unwinding and crash.cpp stack walking not reading lr or r12 after a return. 4) There is no end-to-end measurement; the 0.5-1% figure is an estimate and I did not reproduce it.

title: Production fast path for lifted functions: a compile-time-selected, directly inlined call instead of the LiftRun check wrapper
evidence: src/decomp/lift.cpp:296-321 (LiftRun): in a normal run each lifted call executes a thread_local t_depth test, a function-local static guard for `nested` with two getenv reads at first use, LiftChecking() and DecompOff() (each a function-static guard plus a call into decomp.cpp), LiftEnabled(s.address) (another static guard, a hash lookup when FM2_LIFT_ENABLE is set), and after the call a thread_local t_liftBail test. `lifted` is passed as a PPCFunc* parameter (lift.cpp:296), so the lifted body is called through a pointer and cannot be inlined into the wrapper. The generated wrapper in out/lift/lift_000.cpp (lines 10-24) shows the shape: `static LiftStats s(...); LiftRun(s, ctx, base, __imp__sub_X, lifted_X);`. out/lift/report.tsv: 7,300 functions lifted, 2,727 held back for 'not every branch ran'. The lifted bodies start with `uint32_t v_param_r3 = uint32_t(ctx.r3.u64); const uint64_t w_param_r3 = ...` for every livein register, and for indirect calls set all of r3-r10 from locals (lift_000.cpp, sub_821E4D70).
proposal: Add a `--production` emit mode to lift.py (and make ReXenon's native-link mode, finding 5, the consumer): for functions in the --keep set, emit `PPC_FUNC(sub_X){ lifted_X(ctx, base); }` or better a native-ABI `lifted_X(base, a3, a4)`, with LIFT_BAIL resolved at emit time (the 441 'unchecked-branch' functions fall back by a direct `__imp__sub_X` call) and no LiftStats, TLS or env-var checks. Keep the checker build as it is for validation.
expected_gain: Estimate: about 5-10 ns saved per lifted call (TLS loads, 3-4 static guards, an indirect call), but the dynamic call counts of the lifted set are not measured here, so the total is unknown; the README's own measurement for the replaced C runtime is +5% fps on the benchmark (184-185 vs 176 fps, RTX 4070), which shows lifted code is worth shipping without the wrapper.
risk: Low-medium: the checker build and the production build must be generated from the same lifter output so a function that passed checks is not altered. Only apply to the --keep set.

verify.evidence_checked:
I re-read src/decomp/lift.cpp:296-321 (LiftRun). The code matches the finding. A normal run does a t_depth TLS test, a function-static `nested` guard, LiftChecking(), DecompOff(), LiftEnabled(addr) and a t_liftBail TLS test after the call. The decomp.cpp getters (lines 12-21) are function-static const bools, and LiftEnabled keeps a static `only` pointer, so with no env vars each check is a guard load plus a branch. The lifted body is passed as a PPCFunc* parameter. The generated out/lift/lift_000.cpp has the `static LiftStats s(...); LiftRun(...)` wrapper shape and bodies that load every livein as `v_param_rN`. report.tsv shows 7300 lifted and 2727 held back. lift.py has the --keep mechanism and LIFT_BAIL is a macro in lift.h, so emit-time resolution is feasible. I did not compile anything and did not measure dynamic call counts. Four things weaken it:
1. The cost is guard-byte loads and well-predicted branches (the static-init checks are a load, a compare and a branch), plus one TLS load or two on Windows. That is likely 2-4 ns, not 5-10 ns.
2. No dynamic call count exists for the 7300 lifted functions, so the total gain is unknown.
3. The cited +5% fps (184-185 vs 176) was for the replaced C runtime (CRT), not for lifted functions, so it does not support this gain.
4. This is decomp-branch work and does not touch ReXenon's recompiler. It only matters once the lifted set is shipped.
verify.corrected_gain: Unmeasured. Estimate: 2-4 ns per lifted call (a handful of predicted guard branches and TLS loads). The total depends on how often the lifted functions are called per frame, and no count exists. If the lifted set is hot (say 1M calls per second per core) the saving is about 0.2-0.4% of one core. The +5% fps figure does not apply here.
verify.blockers:
1. Measure dynamic call counts of the lifted functions (a counter in a check build) before ranking this.
2. Only the 7300 kept functions may be changed. The 441 unchecked-branch bodies need an emit-time fallback to `__imp__`, and the checker build must stay byte-identical to the production lifter output.
3. FM2_LIFT_ENABLE and FM2_DECOMP_OFF bisecting would be lost in production mode unless it is kept as a build flag.
4. It lives in the decomp tooling, not the ReXenon fork, so it is out of scope for the recompiler replacement.

title: ReXenon 'native link mode': one ABI tag per function so recompiled, lifted and hand-written code mix cleanly
evidence: Today mixing is done by weak/strong symbol override: recompiled PPC_FUNC_IMPL(__imp__sub_X) plus a weak sub_X alias (recompiler.cpp:2560-2564 under XENON_RECOMP_USE_ALIAS, wrapper at 2624-2628 otherwise); lift.py emits a strong sub_X wrapper (lift.py:1085-1087) that calls the lifted body through LiftRun and keeps `__imp__sub_X` as the fallback original. All three layers use the ctx ABI, so nothing in a lifted function can be called natively by another. lift.py:955-970 also has to scan TU_SUB/PPC_FUNC tokens in src/ to know what is hooked or `taken`, because ReXenon does not publish that. out/lift has 7,300 lifted functions whose bodies are `static void lifted_X(PPCContext&, base)` with params read back out of ctx (lift_000.cpp).
proposal: Design: (1) A single `abi.json` (finding 3) gives each function `{addr, name, tag: native|ctx, params: [...], ret: r3|f1|none|struct, shim: bool, source: recomp|lifted|hook}`. (2) For tag=native, ReXenon emits `fn_X(base, args)` and, only when shim=true, `sub_X(ctx, base)` calling it. (3) For tag=ctx functions (SEH funclets, setjmp users, stack-arg/vararg functions, hooks), a generated adapter `fn_X(base, args) { ctx.r3 = a3; ...; sub_X(ctx, base); return ctx.r3.u32; }` lets native callers call them, so callers never need to know. (4) The lifter targets the same signature (params come from abi.json instead of re-reading livein.json), and a lifted function replaces the recompiled one by taking over the fn_X symbol, with the recompiled body kept as `fn_X__orig` for the check harness. A config flag selects per function: recomp, lifted, or checked. (5) The address-taken/hooked set comes from config + the hooks list, so the lifter no longer greps src/. (6) With a symbol map, emit `// Class::vf3` comments from symbols.txt above each function and a debugger map file (keep sub_ADDR link names because hooks and tools/xexremap.py depend on them).
expected_gain: Enables findings 2 and 5 to be incremental: each lifted or hand-converted function can later be called with no ctx traffic by neighbours, and the old recompiler path can be retired function by function. No standalone fps number; this is the structure that makes the L-effort path reachable (README: 'the road to a build without the recompiled code').
risk: Medium-high design risk: the ABI tag must be proven correct per function, which is why the lift check harness (overlay + twin compare, src/decomp/lift.cpp) should be kept and extended to compare native-ABI results vs. ctx-ABI results for recompiled functions too. Hooks that hand registers through ctx (FM2_SHADOW_ORIGINAL hooks, imports in src/kernel with GUEST_EXPORT reading ctx) always stay ctx-ABI.

verify.evidence_checked: Re-checked the cited code. recompiler.cpp:2559-2564 (alias under XENON_RECOMP_USE_ALIAS) and 2623-2628 (weak wrapper otherwise) match the claim. lift.py:955-970 does grep src/ for TU_SUB and scans build/*/remapped and build/*/generated for PPC_FUNC(sub_X) to build the taken/hooked sets, as stated. lift.py:1085-1087 emits a strong sub_X wrapper that calls LiftRun with __imp__sub_X as the fallback, as stated. out/lift holds 21 files with exactly 7,300 `static void lifted_` bodies. lift_000.cpp reads params back out of ctx (`v_param_r3 = uint32_t(ctx.r3.u64)`). Calls inside lifted code go through ctx: it sets ctx.r3..r10 and uses PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC, and I saw no direct lifted_X() call sites. So the description of the current state is accurate. I did not check the claim that this is an unmet need for the decomp branch. The weak points are that this is a design and architecture proposal with no measured speed gain, it depends on 'finding 3' (abi.json) and on findings 2 and 5, which I could not see, and no per-function ABI correctness evidence was offered. Item (5) is a small, separable cleanup.
verify.corrected_gain: No standalone fps gain. The value is enabling work for the decomp path, which is currently non-incremental. Item (5), taking the hooked/taken set from config instead of grepping src/ and build/, is the only piece that is cheap and independently useful. Treat the full native-ABI scheme as a long-term L-effort project that should not rank above any item with a measurable gain.
verify.blockers: 1) The ABI tag has to be proven correct per function. SEH funclets, setjmp users, varargs and stack-argument functions, and indirect-call targets that read registers all stay on ctx. 2) The finding does not say how a native-ABI function keeps r14-r31 callee-saved semantics or the stack frame (r1) visible to ctx-ABI callees. 3) Anything that checks ctx register state, such as the shadow-original check harness, would have to be re-proven. 4) FM2_SHADOW_ORIGINAL hooks and GUEST_EXPORT imports must stay on ctx. 5) Indirect calls (PPC_CALL_INDIRECT_FUNC) always take the ctx ABI, so every native function needs a ctx shim wherever its address is taken. That shim traffic reduces the gain, and the finding does not count how many call sites are direct versus indirect. 6) It needs abi.json (finding 3) first, which I could not verify.
